lead: Bernoulli's equation is y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)y<sup>n</sup> with n not 0 or 1. The power of y stops it being linear, so an integrating factor cannot be used directly. Dividing by y<sup>n</sup> and substituting z = y<sup>1−n</sup> turn it into a linear equation in z. Solve that with the integrating factor from 1.5, then return to y. It appears in population models with crowding, fluid flow with drag, and circuits with nonlinear parts.
prereq: You need 1.5 Linear first order for the integrating factor, and 1.2 Variables separable for the n = 1 case.

blocks.text: Write the equation in standard form: y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)yn. Here y′ = dy/dx, P(x) and Q(x) are known functions of x, and n is a real number. Work on an interval where y ≠ 0 and the powers are defined. The cases n = 0 and n = 1 are not new. n = 0 gives y′ + Py = Q, which is linear (1.5). n = 1 gives y′ + Py = Qy, which is linear after moving Qy left, or separable (1.2).

For other n, divide by y<sup>n</sup>. This gives y<sup>−n</sup>y′ + P y<sup>1−n</sup> = Q. Put z = y<sup>1−n</sup>. Differentiate: z′ = (1−n)y<sup>−n</sup>y′. So y<sup>−n</sup>y′ = z′/(1−n). Substitute: z′/(1−n) + P z = Q. Multiply by (1−n): z′ + (1−n)P z = (1−n)Q. This is linear in z. The factor (1−n) multiplies both P and Q; losing it is the commonest error.

blocks.where: P(x) and Q(x) are known functions of x; n is a real number; y′ = dy/dx.
z = y<sup>1−n</sup>; P and Q come from the Bernoulli form; n ≠ 0, 1.

sections.h3: Solve the linear equation in z

items: Put the equation in y′ + P y = Q y<sup>n</sup> form; list P, Q and n.
If n = 0 or n = 1, use the earlier methods; do not substitute z.
Divide by y<sup>n</sup>. For n > 0, record that y = 0 is a solution.
Set z = y<sup>1−n</sup>; replace y<sup>−n</sup>y′ by z′/(1−n).
Find μ = e<sup>∫(1−n)P dx</sup>; solve (μ z)′ = μ(1−n)Q.
Integrate, put z = y<sup>1−n</sup> back, simplify; add y = 0 if n > 0.

blocks.text: The integrating factor μ(x) = e<sup>∫(1−n)P dx</sup> makes the left side (μ z)′. After integration, one constant C appears. Back substitution uses z = y<sup>1−n</sup>, so y = z<sup>1/(1−n)</sup>. Check the sign of 1−n: for n = 2 it is negative, for n = −1 it is positive. That sign changes the linear equation and the final power.

sections.h3: Where it is used and the name

blocks.text: Population growth with crowding uses dN/dt = rN − aN², with N(t) the population, r the growth rate and a the crowding constant. This is Bernoulli with n = 2 in the variable N. In a circuit with a nonlinear resistor, the current can obey a Bernoulli equation. In fluid mechanics, the Bernoulli equation is a different statement about energy along a streamline; the family name is the same, but that equation is not in this unit.

examples.question: Solve x dy/dx + y = x² y² for x > 0. Give the general solution and check the branch with C = 1 at x = 2.
steps: Divide by x: dy/dx + y/x = x y². So n = 2, P = 1/x, Q = x.
Set z = y<sup>1−2</sup> = y<sup>−1</sup>. Then z′ = −y<sup>−2</sup>y′. The equation becomes −z′ + z/x = x, so z′ − z/x = −x.
Solve the linear equation in z. The integrating factor is μ = e<sup>∫−dx/x</sup> = 1/x.
Then (z/x)′ = (1/x)(−x) = −1. Integrate: z/x = −x + C, so z = Cx − x².
Back substitute z = 1/y: 1/y = Cx − x², that is y = 1/(Cx − x²).
examples.answer: General solution: 1/y = Cx − x², or y = 1/(Cx − x²). At C = 1, x = 2, y = −0.5.

examples.question: Solve dy/dx + y/x = x y<sup>−1</sup> for x > 0. Give the general solution and check C = 1 at x = 2, taking the positive branch.
steps: Standard form: P = 1/x, Q = x, n = −1.
Divide by y<sup>−1</sup>, which is multiplying by y: y y′ + y²/x = x.
Set z = y<sup>1−(−1)</sup> = y². Then z′ = 2y y′. The equation becomes (1/2)z′ + z/x = x, so z′ + (2/x)z = 2x.
The integrating factor is μ = e<sup>∫2dx/x</sup> = x².
Then (z x²)′ = x²·2x = 2x³. Integrate: z x² = (1/2)x⁴ + C, so z = (1/2)x² + C/x².
Back substitute z = y²: y² = x²/2 + C/x².
Check C = 1, x = 2: y² = 2 + 1/4 = 2.25, so y = 1.5 on the positive branch.
examples.answer: General solution: y² = x²/2 + C/x². At C = 1, x = 2, y = 1.5.

traps: Do not substitute z for n = 0 or n = 1. n = 0 is linear; n = 1 is separable or linear after moving Qy left.
Divide by y<sup>n</sup> before substituting, and put the factor (1−n) on both P and Q. The linear equation is z′ + (1−n)Pz = (1−n)Q, not z′ + Pz = Q.
For n > 0, dividing by y<sup>n</sup> assumes y ≠ 0. The solution y = 0 is genuine and must be added separately.
Back substitution reverses the power: z = y<sup>1−n</sup> gives y = z<sup>1/(1−n)</sup>, not y = z<sup>1−n</sup>. Watch the sign of 1−n.
The Bernoulli equation in fluid mechanics is a different equation. This chapter is only about y′ + P y = Q y<sup>n</sup>.

quiz.q: State the standard form of Bernoulli's equation and the values of n for which the z-substitution is used.
quiz.a: y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)y<sup>n</sup>, with n real and n ≠ 0, 1. The substitution z = y<sup>1−n</sup> is used for n ≠ 0, 1.

quiz.q: Why does dividing by y<sup>n</sup> and setting z = y<sup>1−n</sup> make the equation linear?
quiz.a: Dividing gives y<sup>−n</sup>y′ + P y<sup>1−n</sup> = Q. Since z = y<sup>1−n</sup>, z′ = (1−n)y<sup>−n</sup>y′. So y<sup>−n</sup>y′ becomes z′/(1−n), and y<sup>1−n</sup> becomes z. The result z′ + (1−n)Pz = (1−n)Q has z and z′ to the first power only.

n = 2, P = 1, Q = x. Divide by y²: y<sup>−2</sup>y′ + y<sup>−1</sup> = x. Let z = y<sup>−1</sup>, z′ = −y<sup>−2</sup>y′. Then −z′ + z = x, so z′ − z = −x. IF = e<sup>−x</sup>. Then (z e<sup>−x</sup>)′ = −x e<sup>−x</sup>. Integrate: z e<sup>−x</sup> = (x+1)e<sup>−x</sup> + C, so z = x+1 + C e<sup>x</sup>. Since z = 1/y, 1/y = x+1 + C e<sup>x</sup>.

quiz.q: For n = 2, what solution is lost when dividing by y², and why is it a solution?
quiz.a: The lost solution is y = 0. Substituting y = 0 in y′ + P y = Q y² gives 0 = 0, so it satisfies the equation. Division by y² requires y ≠ 0, so it must be added separately.

quiz.q: For dy/dx + 2y = e<sup>x</sup> y³, list P, Q and n, and write the linear equation in z.
quiz.a: P = 2, Q = e<sup>x</sup>, n = 3. Then 1−n = −2 and z = y<sup>−2</sup>. The linear equation is z′ − 4z = −2e<sup>x</sup>.

quiz.q: Why is n = 1 not solved by the z-substitution?
quiz.a: For n = 1, z = y<sup>1−1</sup> = y<sup>0</sup> = 1, which carries no information about y. The equation y′ + Py = Qy is already linear after moving Qy to the left, or it can be solved as separable.

quiz.q: A student solves dy/dx + y/x = x y<sup>−1</sup> and gets z′ + (2/x)z = 2x with z = y². Check the factor (1−n) and the sign.
quiz.a: Here n = −1, so 1−n = 2. Dividing by y<sup>−1</sup> means multiplying by y: y y′ + y²/x = x. With z = y², z′ = 2y y′, so (1/2)z′ + z/x = x. Multiplying by 2 gives z′ + (2/x)z = 2x. The factor 2 is correct and positive.

beyond: Not for the exam. A Riccati equation y′ = P(x)y² + Q(x)y + R(x) is Bernoulli only when R = 0. With R ≠ 0 it becomes linear only after one particular solution y<sub>1</sub> is known, using z = 1/(y − y<sub>1</sub>). That shifted-reciprocal substitution is related to, but not the same as, z = y<sup>1−n</sup>. In control theory, Bernoulli-type nonlinearities appear in valve flow and transistor models. Search for “logistic equation Bernoulli substitution” and “Riccati equation linearization” to see the next step. When P and Q are measured data rather than formulas, numerical solvers take over.
